image_description: A male mallard duck (drake) standing on a grassy bank near water. The duck features the characteristic iridescent green head, white neck ring, chestnut breast, and grey/brown body plumage. Its yellow bill is clearly visible, as are its orange webbed feet planted in the grass. The background consists of blurred dry branches and water.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The bill is clearly visible, broad, flat, and yellow-green in color, matching the description perfectly.
The eye is visible and appears dark/black, consistent with the taxonomy.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The body shape is robust and streamlined. The plumage texture appears dense and smooth, indicative of waterproof feathers.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image displays the classic male mallard pattern: iridescent green head, distinct white neck ring, chestnut breast, and grey/flank body.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The orange legs are visible. The feet show clear webbing between the toes, and the leg placement is anatomically correct for a duck standing on land.
The folded wing is visible along the side of the body, showing the typical layered feather structure and shape.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The tail is short, and the characteristic upward curl of the central tail feathers (drake feathers) is clearly visible at the rear of the duck.
